title: Blink
goal: An external LED toggles every 0.5 s
pass: GPIO5 toggles at least 4 times within 2.2 s of power-on
learn: GPIO output, FreeRTOS delays
brief:
Write ESP32-S3 firmware with ESP-IDF 5.5:
GPIO5 drives an LED (through a 220Ω resistor, lit when high). Start with it off, then toggle every 500 ms.
Print one line to the serial port on each toggle, e.g. LED ON / LED OFF.
Start blinking right after power-on; don't wait first.
On the bench GPIO5 is also wired to the weather station's buzzer module (for alarms): the buzzer clicking along with the LED is normal.

title: Button
goal: Each BOOT press toggles the LED once
pass: Press BOOT at 0.5 s and 1.0 s (100 ms each): GPIO5 toggles exactly 2 times
learn: GPIO input, interrupts, debouncing
brief:
ESP32-S3, BOOT button on GPIO0 (pulls to ground when pressed, use the internal pull-up).
Each press toggles the LED on GPIO5 between on and off.
Debounce in software (30–50 ms) and don't toggle again on release. A press may be as short as 100 ms, so the debounce window must not be longer than that.
Keep the LED off at power-on; don't blink on your own.
(GPIO5 also has the buzzer module wired in parallel, so a click on each toggle is normal.)

title: Screen
goal: Draw text on the OLED
pass: OLED lights at least 150 pixels and TRYBOARD_OK appears on serial
learn: I2C, frame buffers
brief:
ESP32-S3 with a 0.96″ SSD1306 OLED (128×64): I2C address 0x3C, SDA=GPIO8, SCL=GPIO9.
Initialize the screen and draw two lines of English text, each at least 8 characters (e.g. Hello TryBoard / ESP32-S3 OLED).
When done, print TRYBOARD_OK to serial.

title: Sensors
goal: Read temperature, humidity and pressure
pass: With the environment set to −7.25 ℃ / 88.5 % / 950.12 hPa, every reading line is within ±0.02 ℃ / ±0.1 % / ±0.02 hPa
learn: Sensor compensation formulas, several devices on one I2C bus
brief:
ESP32-S3 with a BME280: I2C address 0x76, SDA=GPIO8, SCL=GPIO9 (other devices may share the bus; only talk to 0x76).
Use the datasheet's compensation formulas (the integer version in section 4.2.3 is recommended), read once per second and print one line each time, in exactly this format:
T=23.50 C H=45.0 % P=1013.25 hPa
(Temperature with two decimals, possibly negative, e.g. T=-7.25 C; humidity with one; pressure with two, in hPa.)

title: Dial
goal: Sweep a servo from 0° to 180°
pass: Within 3 s GPIO4 runs at 50 Hz and the pulse width goes through 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 ms in order
learn: LEDC PWM, pulse width and angle
brief:
ESP32-S3 uses LEDC to output 50 Hz PWM on GPIO4 to drive an SG90 servo.
A 0.5 ms pulse is 0°, 2.5 ms is 180°, linear in between.
Start at 0° right after power-on and step through 0°, 45°, 90°, 135°, 180°, holding each angle for 0.5 s, then loop. Don't add an extra wait at the start.

title: Fit the enclosure
goal: Build a desktop weather station and fit it in a case
pass: At 23.5 ℃: after 1 s the servo pulse settles at 1.675 ms (±0.04), the RGB LED is green, UNIT F appears on serial after pressing BOOT at 2.0 s, and the OLED lights ≥ 300 pixels; the web page also requires an assembly with no warnings (geometric estimate, checked on the web page only)
learn: Combining the earlier checkpoints; why the sensor should stay away from the chip
brief:
Combine the earlier checkpoints into an ESP32-S3 desktop weather station:
· BME280 (0x76) and OLED (0x3C, 128×64) share I2C: SDA=GPIO8, SCL=GPIO9
· Read every 500 ms. The OLED's first line shows the temperature in 2× large text, the second line shows humidity and pressure
· Servo on GPIO4, 50 Hz, pulse width = 0.5 + temperature(℃)/40×2 ms (0–40 ℃ dial; out-of-range values count as 0 or 40 ℃). The servo always uses Celsius and ignores the ℃/℉ toggle
· On-board WS2812 (GPIO48): blue below 18 ℃, green below 28 ℃, otherwise red
· BOOT (GPIO0, pulls to ground when pressed, internal pull-up, 30 ms debounce) toggles ℃/℉, affecting only the OLED; print UNIT F to serial when switching to Fahrenheit and UNIT C when switching back
· Print one line to serial per reading, always in Celsius and in exactly this format: T=23.50 C H=45.0 % P=1013.25 hPa

title: Final project
goal: Pick one of three: Little Yellow who turns around, the lens buddy, or your own idea
pass: Pick a finished project and check it against its pass criteria; you can also write your own
buy: Depends on which one you pick
learn: Define acceptance first, then let the AI write the code
brief:
Pick a finished project: Little Yellow who turns around, the lens buddy, or your own idea.
First spell out what "done" means: which pin, what waveform, what is shown on screen, what is printed to serial.
Give these criteria to the AI together with the requirements.

variants.title: Little Yellow who turns around
variants.goal: Turns, eyes follow, looks back on a button press
variants.buy: 1.28″ GC9A01 round screen, SG90 servo, 3D-printed body
variants.learn: SPI screens, coordinating a servo with a screen
variants.pass: Within 3 s GPIO4 runs at 50 Hz with the pulse width sweeping between 0.83–2.17 ms (±60°); SPIN -60, SPIN +60, EYE R, EYE L appear on serial; after pressing BOOT at 2.6 s LOOK FRONT appears, and at 3 s the eyes are back in the centre (horizontal centroid of the cyan eyes 114–126); the round screen lights ≥ 20000 pixels with ≥ 20000 of yellow face
variants.brief:
Make a turning desktop figure on the ESP32-S3, combining the "Draw the face" and "Turn around" checkpoints:
· GC9A01 round screen (240×240) on SPI2: SCLK=GPIO12, MOSI=GPIO11, CS=GPIO10, DC=GPIO14, RST=GPIO13, backlight GPIO15 (lit when high). Use ESP-IDF's esp_lcd + the espressif/esp_lcd_gc9a01 component; these modules need colour inversion on (esp_lcd_panel_invert_color(true)) and BGR colour order (LCD_RGB_ELEMENT_ORDER_BGR), otherwise the colours are wrong
· Little Yellow's face (coordinates with the screen's top-left corner at 0,0): full-screen yellow #FFC933 background; a dark #141414 rounded-rectangle visor, 148×88, corner radius 32, centred at (120,104); inside the visor two cyan #7CF5FF rounded-rectangle eyes, each 28×56, corner radius 14, centred at (90,104) and (150,104), each with a white highlight of radius 5; below, a dark smile (lower half-arc centred at (120,160), radius 34, line width 6)
· Servo on GPIO4, LEDC 50 Hz: sweep back and forth between 30° and 150° around 90° (±60°), one round trip every 2 s, one step every 20 ms (0.5 ms pulse is 0°, 2.5 ms is 180°). Start turning right after power-on. Print SPIN -60 at the far left and SPIN +60 at the far right
· Eyes follow: when the servo turns in the + direction (pulse widening) both eyes shift 13 pixels right, and 13 pixels left on the way back; move at most 4 pixels per 20 ms. Print EYE R when the eyes reach the far right (+13) and EYE L at the far left (-13). Redrawing only the rows the visor covers is fast enough
· One BOOT press (GPIO0, pulls to ground when pressed, internal pull-up, 50 ms debounce): stop facing front at 90° (1.5 ms pulse), eyes back to centre, print LOOK FRONT; press again to resume turning and print LOOK AROUND

· GC9A01 round screen (240×240) on SPI2: SCLK=GPIO12, MOSI=GPIO11, CS=GPIO10, DC=GPIO14, RST=GPIO13, backlight GPIO15 (lit when high). Use ESP-IDF's esp_lcd + the espressif/esp_lcd_gc9a01 component; these modules need colour inversion on (esp_lcd_panel_invert_color(true)) and BGR colour order (LCD_RGB_ELEMENT_ORDER_BGR), otherwise the colours are wrong

brief:
Add a servo turntable to the "Draw the face" firmware, ESP32-S3:
· Screen wiring and face drawing are the same as in the "Draw the face" checkpoint; draw the face once and keep the eyes looking straight ahead. Wiring: GC9A01 round screen 240×240 on SPI2, SCLK=GPIO12, MOSI=GPIO11, CS=GPIO10, DC=GPIO14, RST=GPIO13, backlight GPIO15, lit when high

goal: A pair of blinking eyes on the round screen
pass: TRYBOARD_OK and BLINK 1 appear on serial within 5.5 s; at the end the round screen has cyan eyes (#7CF5FF ±24) ≥ 5000 pixels with horizontal centroid 112–128, white highlights (#FFFFFF ±24) ≥ 100, pink blush (#FF8FB8 ±24) ≥ 600
buy: ESP32-S3 dev board, 1.28″ GC9A01 round screen
learn: SPI screens, full-frame buffers, simple animation
brief:
Write the eyes of a lens buddy for the ESP32-S3 with ESP-IDF 5.5:
· GC9A01 round screen (240×240) on SPI2: SCLK=GPIO12, MOSI=GPIO11, CS=GPIO10, DC=GPIO14, RST=GPIO13, backlight GPIO15 (lit when high). Use ESP-IDF's esp_lcd + the espressif/esp_lcd_gc9a01 component; these modules need colour inversion on (esp_lcd_panel_invert_color(true)) and BGR colour order (LCD_RGB_ELEMENT_ORDER_BGR), otherwise the colours are wrong
· Black background; a pair of cyan #7CF5FF rounded-rectangle eyes, each 52×84, corner radius 20, centred at (72,112) and (168,112); two white highlights at the top-left of each eye (radius 9 and 4); a pink #FF8FB8 elliptical blush below and outside each eye, centred at (42,170) and (198,170), semi-axes 18×10
· Print TRYBOARD_OK to serial once drawn. Start right after power-on without waiting
· Blinking: once drawn, blink every 3 s. A blink is 6 frames of 30 ms each, with eye height going through 60%, 25%, 5%, 25%, 60%, 100% of the original (shrinking around the eye centre, minimum 8 pixels; no highlights while the height is under half; the blush always stays). After each blink print BLINK <n>, e.g. BLINK 1

title: Enumeration
goal: Plug into a computer and get recognized as a USB keyboard
pass: TRYBOARD_OK appears on serial within 1.5 s; the virtual computer sees the USB device state as "Configured"
buy: ESP32-S3 dev board (with a native USB port), USB-C data cable
learn: Native USB, TinyUSB, device / configuration / HID descriptors
brief:
Write ESP32-S3 firmware with ESP-IDF 5.5 so that it is recognized as a USB keyboard when plugged into a computer (no buttons yet):
· ESP32-S3 native USB (the Type-C port labelled USB / OTG on the board, GPIO19 / GPIO20), using ESP-IDF 5.5's espressif/esp_tinyusb component (TinyUSB)
· Device strings: manufacturer TryBoard, product TryBoard Macro Pad; one HID keyboard interface in the configuration descriptor (boot-protocol keyboard, report descriptor TUD_HID_REPORT_DESC_KEYBOARD)
· Once the computer has finished enumerating (tud_mounted() is true), print TRYBOARD_OK to serial
· Initialize USB right after power-on without waiting; don't send any keys

title: Keys send letters
goal: Press K1 / K2 / K3 to type a / b / c on the computer
pass: Press K1, K2, K3 at 1.2 s, 1.5 s, 1.8 s (100 ms each): the computer's text editor contains exactly abc
learn: GPIO input, debouncing, HID keyboard reports
brief:
Add buttons to the "Enumeration" firmware, ESP32-S3:
· The USB part is exactly the same as in the "Enumeration" checkpoint (product name TryBoard Macro Pad, print TRYBOARD_OK after enumeration)
· Four buttons: K1=GPIO4, K2=GPIO5, K3=GPIO6, K4=GPIO7, other side to ground, using internal pull-ups (low when pressed)
· Software debounce: sample every 10 ms and only accept two matching samples in a row; a press may be as short as 100 ms, so the debounce window must not be longer than that; holding a key counts as one press
· For each character, send a key-down report, then an all-released report, waiting 12 ms after each (the computer polls every 10 ms, so going faster drops characters)
· K1 sends a, K2 sends b, K3 sends c (lowercase, no Shift). Ignore K4 for now
· Print one line to serial per press, e.g. KEY 1 a

title: Combined: macro key
goal: K4 types a whole sentence in one press; fit it in a case
pass: Press K1 at 1.2 s and K4 at 1.5 s (100 ms each): the computer types exactly a and "Hello TryBoard" followed by a newline; the web page also requires an assembly with no warnings (geometric estimate, checked on the web page only)
learn: Macros: one key sends a series of reports; combining the previous two checkpoints
brief:
Combine the "Enumeration" and "Keys send letters" checkpoints into a small USB keypad, ESP32-S3:
· The USB part is the same as in the "Enumeration" checkpoint (product name TryBoard Macro Pad, print TRYBOARD_OK after enumeration)
· Four buttons: K1=GPIO4, K2=GPIO5, K3=GPIO6, K4=GPIO7, other side to ground, using internal pull-ups (low when pressed)
· Software debounce: sample every 10 ms and only accept two matching samples in a row; a press may be as short as 100 ms, so the debounce window must not be longer than that; holding a key counts as one press
· For each character, send a key-down report, then an all-released report, waiting 12 ms after each (the computer polls every 10 ms, so going faster drops characters)
· K1 / K2 / K3 still send a / b / c
· K4 is the macro key: one press types Hello TryBoard followed by Enter (capital letters need Left Shift; Enter is HID keycode 0x28) and prints MACRO Hello TryBoard to serial
· Don't drop keys while typing the macro: wait for tud_hid_ready() before every character

title: Light the strip
goal: 8 LEDs light up one by one in warm white
pass: LAMP ON 8 appears on serial within 1.5 s; WS2812 on GPIO5 gets at least 8 frames (lighting one by one), and in the last frame all 8 are lit, all #40260C (±2 per channel)
learn: RMT transmit, WS2812 timing, GRB order
brief:
Write ESP32-S3 firmware with ESP-IDF 5.5:
· 8-LED WS2812 strip: DIN to GPIO5 (level-shifted to 5 V through a 74AHCT125), 5V / GND to the dev board's 5V / GND. On the wire it is GRB order at 800 kHz: a 0 bit is 0.3 µs high, 0.9 µs low; a 1 bit is 0.9 µs high, 0.3 µs low; one frame is 8 × 24 bits, with the line held low ≥ 280 µs between frames. ESP-IDF's built-in RMT transmit driver (driver/rmt_tx.h) with rmt_new_bytes_encoder is enough; the led_strip component isn't needed
· Light them one by one right after power-on: one more LED every 60 ms, and once all 8 are lit print LAMP ON 8 to serial. The colour is warm white #FF9933 at 64/255 brightness: each channel = original value × 64 / 255 (integer division), i.e. R=64 G=38 B=12 (#40260C). Send 0 for unlit LEDs
· Once lit, keep it steady; don't blink again

title: Read the knob
goal: With the lights on, report on serial how many detents the knob turned and how many times it was pressed
pass: Turn 3 detents clockwise at 0.6 s, 5 counter-clockwise at 1.0 s, press for 100 ms at 1.4 s: KNOB 3, KNOB -2, PRESS 1 appear on serial; the strip is still 8 LEDs at #40260C (±2)
learn: PCNT quadrature counting, debouncing mechanical buttons
brief:
Add a knob to the "Light the strip" firmware, ESP32-S3:
· Strip wiring, lighting one by one at power-on and LAMP ON 8 are the same as in the "Light the strip" checkpoint
· EC11 rotary encoder module: CLK=GPIO6, DT=GPIO7, SW=GPIO15 (pulls to ground when pressed, enable the internal pull-up). Use PCNT (driver/pulse_cnt.h) configured like the ESP-IDF example peripherals/pcnt/rotary_encoder: two channels, channel A edge on GPIO6 and level on GPIO7, channel B edge on GPIO7 and level on GPIO6, 4× decoding, ±100 as the limits with accum_count on, 1 µs glitch filter. That way clockwise increases the count, 4 counts per detent
· Check every 10 ms: detents = count / 4; when it changes print KNOB <detents> (may be negative, e.g. KNOB -2)
· Debounce the button in software for 20–50 ms (a press may be as short as 100 ms, so the debounce window must not be longer than that); print PRESS <n> on each press, nothing on release
· In this checkpoint the knob doesn't change the lights

title: Combined: knob lamp
goal: Turn the knob to adjust brightness; press it to adjust colour instead
pass: 2 detents clockwise at 0.5 s gives LEVEL 6; press at 0.9 s gives MODE color; 2 detents clockwise at 1.3 s gives COLOR 2 green; press at 1.7 s gives MODE level; 5 detents clockwise at 2.0 s gives LEVEL 8 (stops at the top); in the last frame all 8 LEDs are #108020 (±2 per channel); the web page also requires an assembly with no warnings (geometric estimate, checked on the web page only)
learn: State machines: the same knob does different things in two modes
brief:
Combine the "Light the strip" and "Read the knob" checkpoints into a knob lamp, ESP32-S3:
· Strip and knob wiring are the same as in the "Read the knob" checkpoint (strip DIN=GPIO5; encoder CLK=GPIO6, DT=GPIO7, SW=GPIO15, PCNT 4× decoding, clockwise increases the count, 4 counts per detent)
· Light one by one at power-on: one more LED every 60 ms, and once all 8 are lit print LAMP ON 8. At power-on the colour is warm white at brightness level 4
· Brightness level L goes from 1 to 8, starting at 4; the colour table has 6 entries, starting at 0: 0 warm #FF9933, 1 red #FF2020, 2 green #20FF40, 3 blue #2040FF, 4 purple #C040FF, 5 white #FFFFFF. All 8 LEDs are always the same colour: each channel = colour value × (L × 16) / 255 (integer division), e.g. warm white at L=4 is #40260C
· Two modes, starting in brightness mode: in brightness mode each detent changes L by 1 (stops at 1 or 8), printing LEVEL <L> on each change; in colour mode each detent moves to the next / previous colour (wrapping), printing COLOR <number> <name>, e.g. COLOR 2 green
· Pressing the knob (20–50 ms debounce, a press may be as short as 100 ms) switches modes, printing MODE color or MODE level
· Refresh the strip as soon as brightness or colour changes; don't add an extra wait at the start

title: Distance printout
goal: Measure distance every 0.1 s and print it to serial
pass: Obstacle at 42 cm first, removed at 1.2 s: every distance line reads 42.0 ± 0.3 cm, at least 8 lines; after removal DIST --- appears on serial
buy: ESP32-S3 dev board, HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, one 1 kΩ and one 2 kΩ resistor (voltage divider)
learn: Measuring pulse width with RMT receive; 5 V parts on 3.3 V pins need a voltage divider
brief:
Write ESP32-S3 firmware with ESP-IDF 5.5:
· HC-SR04 (5 V supply): Trig=GPIO17, Echo to GPIO18 through a 1 kΩ / 2 kΩ divider (Echo is 5 V and will damage the GPIO without one). Measure every 100 ms: drive Trig high for 10 µs; Echo high time (µs) × 343 m/s ÷ 2 is the distance, rounded to 0.1 cm (e.g. 2449 µs gives 42.0 cm). RMT receive (driver/rmt_rx.h, 1 MHz resolution, signal_range_max_ns = 25 ms) is recommended for measuring Echo width; a GPIO interrupt plus esp_timer also works. With nothing in front, Echo stays high for about 38 ms before falling: a width over 25 ms, or nothing measured within 60 ms, counts as no reading
· Print one line to serial per measurement, in exactly this format: DIST 42.0 cm (one decimal); print DIST --- when there is no reading
· Start measuring right after power-on without waiting

title: OLED display
goal: Show the distance in large text with a distance bar below
pass: Obstacle at 42 cm: every reading line is 42.0 ± 0.3 cm; OLED lights ≥ 300 pixels
learn: I2C, monochrome frame buffers, bundling your own font
brief:
Add an OLED to the "Distance printout" firmware, ESP32-S3:
· Ranging wiring, method and print format are the same as in the "Distance printout" checkpoint (Trig=GPIO17, Echo to GPIO18 through the divider; DIST 42.0 cm / DIST ---)
· SSD1306 OLED (128×64): I2C address 0x3C, SDA=GPIO8, SCL=GPIO9 (400 kHz). Refresh after each measurement: write the distance on the first line in 2× large text (5×7 font scaled to 10×14), e.g. 42.0 cm, or --- cm when there is no reading; below it draw a distance bar: outline 128×12 (starting at y=44), with the filled part's width = distance(cm) × 128 / 200 (over 200 cm counts as 200)
· ESP-IDF has no fonts, so bring your own 5×7 bitmap font

title: Combined: parking-sensor ruler
goal: The closer it gets, the faster the buzzer beeps; too close and it beeps continuously
pass: Obstacle at 60 cm first, moved to 15 cm at 1.5 s and to 150 cm at 2.5 s: GPIO5 is 2.7 kHz with 0–50% duty; 2–5 beeps in 0.3–1.5 s, 4–9 beeps in 1.8–2.5 s (faster), silent in 2.8–3.2 s; DIST 15.0 cm appears on serial; OLED lights ≥ 300 pixels; the web page also requires an assembly with no warnings (geometric estimate, checked on the web page only)
learn: Square waves from LEDC; coordinating ranging and sound in two tasks
brief:
Combine the "Distance printout" and "OLED display" checkpoints into an ultrasonic ruler that beeps (a parking sensor), ESP32-S3:
· Ranging and OLED are exactly the same as in the "OLED display" checkpoint (Trig=GPIO17, Echo to GPIO18 through the divider; OLED 0x3C, SDA=GPIO8, SCL=GPIO9; serial DIST 42.0 cm / DIST ---)
· Passive buzzer module I/O on GPIO5: LEDC outputs a 2700 Hz square wave, 50% duty while sounding and 0 duty while silent (don't stop the LEDC timer or switch the pin to another function)
